newsitem.title: FRANCE: Strife-torn Renault plunges into the red.
newsitem.headline: Strife-torn Renault plunges into the red.

text.p: French carmaker Renault reported a $923 million loss for 1996 Thursday, its first in 10 years, after taking a 3.9 billion franc ($690 million) charge to close down a Belgian plant and cut nearly 2,800 jobs in France.

Belgian workers protesting the closure clashed with French police when they tried to prevent car deliveries from a depot in the town of Wavrin in northern France. Workers also demonstrated outside Renault's Paris headquarters during a board meeting.
Chairman Louis Schweitzer said the board of the company, which is 46 percent owned by the French government, had approved the plant shutdown and job cutbacks.
But the company increased the provision set aside for the closure to 2.8 billion francs ($491 million) to cushion the blow for the plant's 3,100 workers through accompanying measures.

Even excluding the restructuring charges, Renault had an operating loss of 1.77 billion francs ($311 million), compared with a year-earlier operating profit of 1.20 billion ($211 million), as both its car and truck operations lost money.
"The car division was especially hurt by a price war that spread in France during a year of major model renewal," the company said in a statement.
The industrial vehicles division had a loss in 1996, because U.S. and European truck sales fell. The division owns Mack Trucks.
"In the United States, that (downturn) was expected, but in Europe it was not," Schweitzer said. "We were expecting a recovery but it stalled."
The truck business is expected to keep losing money and will be the focus of more cost-cutting measures, he said, adding that they would not be spectacular.

In Paris, about 100 Renault workers demonstrated outside the company's headquarters. Police also turned away a group of workers who tried to enter the company's prestige showroom on the Champs-Elysees avenue.
But workers have so far shown lukewarm response to union calls for labour action despite a reputation for militancy.
Renault, the smallest of the six companies producing a full range of cars in Europe, has cut its work force by around 40,000 in the past 10 years to just under 141,000 at the end of 1996.
